extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral and political philosophy; scholars interested in ethics, natural right, and theory of the state
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize the evaluative principles and normative standards Schopenhauer gives for right and wrong, property, contract, state, and punishment as presented in this chapter of a metaphysical-ethical treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong (general definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrong is that quality of conduct in which an individual extends the assertion of the will appearing in his own body so far that it becomes the denial of the will appearing in the bodies of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer frames wrong as the assertion of one’s will to the point of denying another’s will; it is a moral determination relating to action (the expression of will) and is accompanied in the wrong-doer by an inward pain (remorse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees and types of wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrong expresses itself in gradations from the highest (cannibalism) to murder, mutilation/injury, subjugation/slavery, and seizure of another's goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cannibalism is the most distinct type (greatest conflict of the will with itself), murder follows, then injury/mutilation (differing only in degree), then subjugation and seizure of goods (theft is related to slavery when goods are fruits of another's labour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remorse / feeling of wrong committed
rubrics_metrics.description: The knowledge of wrong presents itself instantly as an obscure feeling called remorse or the feeling of 'wrong committed'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remorse is the inner consciousness signaling the excessive assertion of will; murder is followed 'instantly and with fearful distinctness' by remorse—it inflicts a lifelong wound on peace of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property right based on labour
rubrics_metrics.description: All true (moral) right of property is based simply and solely on work; property not taken without wrong can only be that which has been produced by a person's own powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Laws of Manu to illustrate: cultivated land belongs to the one who cleared and ploughed it; mere avowal or prior enjoyment without improvement gives no moral title to exclusive possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity of right of preoccupation (first-occupation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The so-called right of preoccupation—exclusive future enjoyment claimed from mere past enjoyment or first occupancy—is morally without foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If family hunted a district without improving it, they cannot morally prevent a newcomer from also hunting there; first occupation alone, or mere enjoyment, does not justify exclusive future rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferability of moral property rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The morally established right of property gives to the owner of a thing the same unlimited power over it as over his own body, so he can part with possessions by exchange or gift, and transferees possess them with the same moral right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property founded on labour confers the owner's legitimate power to dispose of it; voluntary surrender or reward (within a community/state) can also establish transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong through violence and wrong through craft (lie): moral equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrong occurs either through violence or through craft (falsifying knowledge/the lie); both are morally essential the same because both aim at compelling another to serve one's will instead of his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violence uses physical causality; craft uses motivation/knowledge to present illusive motives. The lie always aims at influencing another's will; empty boasting, broken promises, and deception are forms of wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: The lie defined as wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: Every imposing of a lie is a wrong because it falsifies another's knowledge to move his will and thereby extends the liar's authority over another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: directing a traveller to a false road is wrong; mere refusal to tell (withholding) is not necessarily wrong; the most complete lie is the broken contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken contract as the most complete lie
rubrics_metrics.description: When promises are deliberately exchanged and one party breaks the covenant, he has deceived the other by introducing illusory motives, thereby committing a distinct wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the promise is the motive for reciprocal performance, breaking it extends control of one's will to another and undermines the moral basis of contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of compulsion / self-defence
rubrics_metrics.description: Warding off an attempted wrong cannot itself be wrong and is therefore right; if another's assertion of will denies that essential to my person, I have a right to deny that denial with necessary force (right of compulsion), possibly extending to killing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warding off is 'negation of the negation'—an assertion of one's own will as embodied—so defensive violence (proportionate to the threat) is morally permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to lie within scope of compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases where I have a right of compulsion, I also have a right to use craft (lies) to oppose the other's violence; 'a man acts with perfect right who assures a highway robber ... that he has nothing more upon him.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: deceiving a burglar into a cellar to trap him, using false dice against someone who stole from you, deceiving captors to regain freedom—craft is justifiable where one is entitled to resist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between moral (ethical) right and juridical (positive) right
rubrics_metrics.description: Right and wrong are moral determinations valid for the consideration of human action as expression of will (ethics); when transferred to the passive side (suffering) for legislation, ethical right becomes juridical right (positive law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethics concerns inner disposition and conscience; the state concerns outward deeds and suffering. The state applies inverted ethics to prevent suffering by law and punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin and aim of the state (contract to avoid suffering)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state arises from a contract in which individuals renounce inflicting wrong in order to diminish or suppress the suffering of wrong; its aim is well-being (salus publica) rather than furthering inner morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state exists because reason recognizes that individual pleasures from harming are outweighed by others' suffering; the state enforces negative rights to protect against suffering, not to make people moral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of what the state can and cannot secure
rubrics_metrics.description: The state can enforce negative rights (preventing suffering of wrong) but cannot enforce benevolent, positive obligations of love or produce the phenomenology of mutual well-wishing; only negative duties can be exacted by force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because benevolence requires active assumption of costs, the state cannot require universal active love—only prohibitions and enforcement of non-harmful conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for just positive legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive legislation is just (a positive right and a state based upon right) only if, in essential matters, it is throughout determined in accordance with the pure theory of right and each of its propositions can be grounded in that theory; otherwise it is a 'positive wrong' (despotism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When legislation lacks grounding in moral right, it becomes enforced wrong (examples: serfdom, vassalage). The pure theory of right supplies foundations for legislation (property, contracts, state aim, punishment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal points the doctrine of right must supply
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important points for legislation: (1) explanation of inner significance of right/wrong and application in ethics, (2) deduction of the law of property, (3) deduction of moral validity of contracts, (4) explanation of origin and aim of the state and inversion for legislation, (5) deduction of the right of punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the philosophical foundations upon which positive law should be built; remaining legal doctrine is application and definition of limits for life relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of punishment depends on positive law and aims at deterrence
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no right of punishment apart from the state; all right to punish is based on positive law which before the offence has determined a punishment; the immediate end of punishment is the fulfilment of the law as a contract and deterrence of future infringements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment is forward-looking (deterrence). It differs from revenge, which is backward-looking and aimed only at requital; punishment must be enforced according to law to be effective as counter-motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of punishment-as-requital (jus talionis) as moral justification
rubrics_metrics.description: The requital of wrong by infliction of pain without aim for the future (revenge) is wicked and cannot be morally justified; Kant's theory of punishment as mere requital is groundless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment cannot be justified as expiation or neutralization of past crime alone; moral legitimacy comes from public safety and deterrence arranged by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of the punished person as means in service of public security
rubrics_metrics.description: When punishment is inflicted in fulfilment of the law for public security, the punished criminal must, with complete right, be used as a mere means to re-establish public security (contrary to an absolute Kantian prohibition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer argues that using the criminal as a means (e.g., executing a murderer) is justified because public security—the chief end of the state—requires carrying out law to deter future crimes.
